newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-Australia Treasury chief warns on debt.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Australia Treasury chief warns on debt.

text.p: The Australian government's senior economic advisor, Treasury Secretary Ted Evans, on Monday warned that the nation's debt levels would remain dangerously high unless the government delivered its planned budget cuts.

"One does not need to predict an impending world downturn to recognise the more pertinent point that allowing net debt to remain at the level now reached would be courting danger," Evans told a business economists' luncheon in Sydney.
"This is the consideration, more than any other, which imparts urgency to the fiscal consolidation task," he said.

The Australian government's net debt to GDP ratio had jumped to about 19 percent in 1996 from around four percent in 1991 and had been projected to rise to almost 20 percent without the fiscal tightening announced in last month's budget, he said.
"It would be difficult to escape the conclusion that an upward trend is well established and, without substantial fiscal consolidation, is likely to continue," he said.
"It is in this sense already a problem."

The new Liberal-National conservative coalition government announced in its 1996/97 budget in August cuts to the budget deficit in the current year to June 30, 1997 worth A$3.9 billion (US$3.07 billion) to reduce the deficit to A$5.6 billion.
The government also said it aimed to bring the budget into underlying surplus, which excludes the effects of asset sales, by 1998/99.
Evans said this planned budget tightening would be quite an achievement.
"In addition, the government committed itself to a longer term strategy which seeks an underlying balance in the government's accounts 'over the (economic) cycle'," he said.
"This approach introduces a balance sheet anchor and raises a new benchmark: namely that Commonwealth net debt, in future, will not be increased 'over the cycle'," Evans added.

Evans' comments echo those of Treasurer Peter Costello in his budget night speech when he said budget inaction would leave Australia dangerously exposed to shifts in the international outlook or sentiment.
Evans said this budget cutting programme could continue at the same time as robust growth.
He also said company profits remained strong and therefore the Treasury's business investment forecast of 14 percent growth in 1996/97 was justified.
"This course can be pursued as now proposed, while continuing to enjoy quite robust growth in the short term," he said.
"They (profits) may not be growing as strongly, but they're at quite high levels," Evans said.
While the manufacturing and housing sectors were showing some weakness both in terms of output and profits, other industries continued to perform well.
"Beyond that, the weakness is not there. It's not there in mining, for example, and it's not there in services."
Evans however warned that the wages outlook remained uncertain and wage increases must be underpinned by productivity improvements.
He also said the fast-growing services sector remained lightly taxed.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
